title: 'Instant effect' is a contested way to describe entanglement
summary: The v1 sentence that measuring one particle instantly affects the other is an interpretation, not the experimental result.
body: The v1 quantum article said entangled particles are correlated so that measuring one instantly affects the other, and attributed the discomfort to Einstein. The 1935 EPR paper argues about completeness. Aspect's 1982 experiment reports correlations that violate a Bell inequality. Whether those correlations should be described as an instantaneous influence is disputed across interpretations. Standard quantum theory is also taught as forbidding controllable faster-than-light signaling. This card keeps the experimental result and the popular wording apart.

contested_views.label: Influence language
contested_views.summary: Popular and some philosophical descriptions still say a measurement instantly affects the distant outcome. That wording is not forced by the 1982 paper's title, which reports a violation of Bell's inequalities.
